summary: This proposed standard defines a MIB, a set of managed objects for network management tools such as SNMP, for monitoring RIP version 2 on routers. It was replaced by RFC 1724.

eli5.summary: Network managers need a standard way to ask a router how it is doing. This paper lists the questions they can ask about one particular route-sharing feature.

questions: what is the rip version 2 mib
which snmp objects does rip-2 define
is the rip2 peer table mandatory
subtitle: The SNMP objects a router exposes so managers can watch and configure RIP version 2.

tldr.problem: Network managers had no standard set of SNMP objects for monitoring and configuring RIP version 2 on a router.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module, rip2, with global counters, per-interface status and configuration tables, and an optional peer table.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard and has been replaced by RFC 1724.

today: RFC 1389 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 1724, which is the version to use.

sections.title: Where This MIB Fits
sections.content:
RFC 1389 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing RIP Version 2 in TCP/IP-based internets. It builds on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework, which has three parts: the SMI (RFC 1155 and the more concise RFC 1212) for describing and naming objects, MIB-II (RFC 1213) as the core set of managed objects, and SNMP (RFC 1157) as the protocol used to reach those objects.

Each object has a name, a syntax and an encoding. The name is an object identifier, and the syntax is written in the restricted subset of ASN.1 that the SMI allows.
sections.eli5: There is already a rulebook for how to ask devices questions. This memo adds a new chapter just for the route-sharing feature called RIP-2.

sections.title: Structure of the RIP-2 MIB
sections.content:
The MIB has three parts. Global counters help detect the harmful effects of RIP incompatibilities. An interfaces table holds interface-specific statistics and configuration. An optional neighbor (peer) table holds information that may help when debugging neighbor relationships.

The module hangs off rip2, which is { mib-2 23 }. Like RIP version 2 itself, the MIB takes care to preserve compatibility with RIP-1 systems. Because RIP versions 1 and 2 do not deal with addressless links, a RIP interface here is assumed to be a subnet within a routing domain.

Implementation of the global group and the interface groups is mandatory for systems that implement RIP-2. The peer group is optional.
sections.eli5: The MIB is a dashboard with three panels: totals for the whole router, a panel for each network the router is attached to, and an optional list of neighbors.

sections.title: Textual Conventions
sections.content:
Two new data types are introduced as textual conventions. Validation is the standard "set to invalid causes deletion" type, with values valid(1) and invalid(2). RouteTag represents the contents of the Route Tag field in the packet header or route entry, and is defined as an OCTET STRING (SIZE (2)).

The RFC stresses that these conventions only improve readability. Objects defined with them are still encoded by the rules of the primitive type, so no change to the SMI or SNMP is needed.
sections.eli5: These are nicknames for kinds of answers, like calling a yes/no switch a Validation. They make the list easier to read without changing how anything is sent.

sections.title: Counters, Interface Tables and the Peer Table
sections.content:
The globals have two counters: rip2GlobalRouteChanges counts changes RIP made to the IP route database, and rip2GlobalQueries counts responses sent to RIP queries from other systems.

The interface status table is indexed by the interface address. It counts RIP response packets that were discarded for any reason (rip2IfStatRcvBadPackets), routes ignored in valid packets (rip2IfStatRcvBadRoutes) and triggered updates actually sent (rip2IfStatSentUpdates, which explicitly excludes full updates containing new information). Writing invalid to rip2IfStatStatus deletes the interface.

The interface configuration table has settings such as the routing domain value (rip2IfConfDomain), the authentication type (noAuthentication or simplePassword), the authentication key, what to send and receive, and a default metric from 0 to 15. A default metric of zero means no default route is originated, though one learned via another router may still be propagated. The authentication key is up to 16 octets, padded on the right with nulls, and reading it always returns a zero-length string so that authentication cannot be bypassed by reading the MIB.

The optional peer table is indexed by peer address and domain. It records when the last update arrived (rip2PeerLastUpdate, from sysUpTime), the RIP version in the last packet header, and counts of bad packets and bad routes from that peer.
sections.eli5: There are tally counters for mistakes and updates, and a settings panel for each network, including a password that you can set but never read back. A peer list shows who the neighbors are and when they last spoke.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The only security-related design detail in the module itself is that the authentication key object always reads back as an empty string, and that the authentication type can be set to simplePassword on an interface.
sections.eli5: The memo does not talk about security, except that the secret password can never be read out of the box.
